comparison: Both strongly support the core allocentric coding finding (C2-C4, C15, C18-C20, C29-C30, C66-C67). OpenEval emphasizes quantitative evidence and statistical rigor, while peer reviewers describe the evidence as 'compelling' and note all three reviewers affirmed this finding. Both evaluations are SUPPORTED with high confidence.

Both support the time-dependent memory decay findings (C24-C26). OpenEval notes appropriate statistical testing and consistency with literature, while peer reviewer explicitly affirms the waiting period manipulation and interpretation. Both evaluations are SUPPORTED.

Perfect agreement on attentional requirements (C32-C34). Both evaluations are SUPPORTED. OpenEval describes the dual-task paradigm as well-designed with clear statistical evidence, while peer reviewer explicitly confirms the finding that path integration requires attentional effort.

Both support vestibular sufficiency claims (C35-C39). OpenEval emphasizes bidirectional manipulation and statistical comparisons, while peer reviewer acknowledges the systematic manipulation of vestibular input. OpenEval also addresses task-independence (C40-C41) which peer reviewer includes in the same evaluation.

OpenEval supports task-independence (C40-C41) with emphasis on convergent evidence across perception and action measures. Peer reviewer includes these claims in broader acceptance of systematic manipulations but does not specifically highlight task-independence as a separate finding.

Perfect agreement on horizontal-vertical asymmetry (C6, C42-C51). Both evaluations are SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes the clever experimental design and quantitative match between fitted and actual distances, while peer reviewer explicitly confirms the asymmetry finding and its resemblance to animal locomotion.

Perfect agreement on comparative claims with desert ants (C7, C52-C54). Both evaluations are SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes appropriate citations and meaningful cross-species comparison, while peer reviewer explicitly affirms the resemblance to animal locomotion control.

Disagreement on angular accuracy claims (C27-C28). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED based on regression analysis with high r² values, while peer reviewer rates UNCERTAIN, questioning whether perceived size should be 'lifted up' in walking condition but observing it remained at same height as baseline.

Both rate functional advantage claims (C55-C61) as UNCERTAIN. OpenEval notes these are theoretical predictions rather than empirically tested results, while peer reviewer suggests alternative 'compensation mechanism' interpretation, indicating the functional interpretation may not be the only explanation.

Disagreement on competing hypotheses (C86-C89). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, stating predictions are clearly articulated and logically derived, while peer reviewer rates UNCERTAIN, expressing confusion about how allocentric hypothesis is operationalized in Figure 2b, questioning whether perceived object depending on observer's new location is consistent with allocentric coding.

Both address neural speculation (C69-C76 for OpenEval, C70-C74 for peer). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN, noting these are speculative hypotheses without neural data. Peer reviewer rates SUPPORTED, stating the revised version 'effectively situates the research' and 'offers a clearer explanation for the potential neurological basis,' suggesting acceptance of speculation as appropriately contextualized.

OpenEval rates predictions about richer visual environments (C62-C65) as UNCERTAIN, noting this is acknowledged speculation without empirical testing. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific claims.

OpenEval supports background claims about ground-based spatial coding and integration model (C8-C14, C78-C85) as well-established prior work. No specific peer review evaluation addresses these foundational claims separately.

OpenEval supports path-integration mechanism description (C15-C17, C77) as accurately describing established literature. No specific peer review evaluation addresses these theoretical framework claims separately, though C15 appears in peer R1 as part of broader allocentric coding evaluation.
OpenEval supports motivating phenomenon and functional significance (C1, C68). No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these framing claims.
